items.stem: A Massachusetts nonsterile-compounding pharmacy uses an established master formulation record for a 100-mL oral suspension. A new patient-specific preparation follows the same formula, but uses different ingredient LOTS and is prepared by a different qualified compounder. Under the Board's inspection expectations and applicable USP <795> record framework, which records are appropriate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Use only the master formulation record for all subsequent batches, because batch-specific details are already established by the first successful preparation.
choices.why: Incorrect. The Board's retail inspection template requires a compounding record for every nonsterile preparation; an MFR is not a substitute for recording later lots and personnel.

choices.text: Follow the established master formulation record and prepare a separate compounding record identifying the ingredients and lot information actually used for this preparation.
choices.why: Correct. The reusable MFR describes the formulation and method; the preparation-specific CR captures this batch's ingredients, lot numbers and execution details.

choices.text: Create a completely new master formulation solely because the same approved formula is made for a different patient's prescription.
choices.why: Incorrect. A change of patient does not by itself require inventing a different formulation when the existing MFR remains applicable.

choices.text: Document the actual preparation date, compounder, measurements and finished preparation details in a compounding record linked to the correct formulation.
choices.why: Correct. Massachusetts inspection standards require an MFR to be followed and a CR for each preparation, making the record traceable to the particular operation.

items.citation: 247 CMR 9.01(3); MA Board Retail Pharmacy Inspection Template items 92–93; USP <795> §§8–9, master formulation and compounding records
items.novelty_rationale: New component lots and compounder change the preparation-specific record, not the underlying formula; Board inspection template directly supports requirement.

items.stem: A Massachusetts sterile compounding pharmacy formerly produced Category 2 NONHAZARDOUS CSPs under a validated ISO Class 5 primary engineering control (PEC) inside a properly classified cleanroom suite. After renovation, the same PEC is moved into an UNCLASSIFIED segregated compounding area (SCA) while all personnel qualifications remain current. Management proposes assigning the same Category 2 refrigerated BUDs as before solely because the hood still meets ISO Class 5. What is the best response?

choices.text: Keep the old BUDs, since the ISO Class 5 primary airflow is the only relevant classification for every CSP category.
choices.why: Incorrect. The surrounding environmental classification and location requirements matter; ISO 5 PEC status alone does not preserve every Category 2 environmental condition.

choices.text: Apply the old BUDs if staff have passed their competency evaluations, because trained staff replace the need for a classified buffer room.
choices.why: Incorrect. Personnel competency is required but does not substitute for the facility's engineering and environmental standards.

choices.text: Requalify the changed facility and reassess category and BUD; an ISO 5 PEC in an SCA does not retain Category 2 BUDs automatically.
choices.why: Correct. An ISO 5 PEC in an SCA is not the same environment as a classified cleanroom suite for default Category 2 limits; changes require qualification and reassessment.

choices.text: Use the maximal Category 2 BUD whenever preparations contain only sterile manufactured ingredients, regardless of room classification.
choices.why: Incorrect. Sterile starting components and a certified PEC do not independently grant Category 2 BUD authority absent the required setting and controls.

items.novelty_rationale: Facility move from classified cleanroom suite to an SCA changes category/BUD rather than merely staff qualifications.

items.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy conducts its controlled-substance stock reconciliation and finds 10 Schedule II tablets missing. The pharmacist immediately confirms that EIGHT tablets were actually dispensed under a documented prescription but posted to the wrong inventory record. The remaining TWO tablets cannot yet be accounted for, and there is no confirmed theft, diversion or significant loss determination. Under MA Board Policy 2026-01, what is the BEST next action regarding the Board loss report?

choices.text: File a Board confirmed-theft report for all ten tablets immediately, because any first discrepancy automatically establishes employee diversion.
choices.why: Incorrect. Initial discrepancy alone does not establish theft or confirmed loss; eight units have already been traced to a posting error.

choices.text: Treat the discrepancy as fully resolved because finding one record error proves every missing unit has the same cause.
choices.why: Incorrect. Two tablets remain unexplained and require further inventory reconciliation and assessment; unrelated errors cannot be assumed to explain them.

choices.text: Ignore the two tablets until the next annual inventory because a quantity below three tablets is never significant.
choices.why: Incorrect. The policy does not set a blanket 'three tablet' exemption; unexplained discrepancies require investigation and significance assessment.

choices.text: Investigate and record the remaining two tablets, and determine whether a reportable loss is confirmed under applicable rules.
choices.why: Correct. MA Board Policy 2026-01 states not to submit unconfirmed loss reports, but still requires action for confirmed theft/diversion or significant losses; DEA and other agencies have distinct rules.

items.citation: MA Board Policy 2026-01 §§II–III (adopted Mar. 26, 2026); 21 CFR 1301.76(b) (distinct federal reporting rule)
items.novelty_rationale: Different from general 24h/7d reporting: distinguish a partially reconciled inventory discrepancy from a confirmed theft, and do not merge Board with DEA deadlines.

items.stem: A licensed Massachusetts hospital pharmacy receives two controlled-drug transactions from a nursing unit: Transaction X is an INTact, fully accountable Schedule II dosage unit that was never administered. Transaction Y is a partially used Schedule II injectable dose whose remaining portion is to be discarded after a documented patient administration. All identities and authorizations are valid. Which handling practices are appropriate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Document X's return from nursing-unit custody to pharmacy custody, reconciling the nursing-unit and pharmacy-controlled inventory records.
choices.why: Correct. An unused accountable unit returned to stock custody is an inventory movement that requires traceability at both locations.

choices.text: Combine X's unused unit with Y's partially used residual and enter both as a single patient waste event.
choices.why: Incorrect. An intact unused return and a partially administered dose/waste have different origins; merging their records defeats inventory accountability.

choices.text: Document Y's administered amount and witnessed waste under institutional policy, with the applicable licensed witness and reconciliation of the unit-dose record.
choices.why: Correct. Hospital controlled-drug accountability requires recording administered/wasted quantities and the witness, rather than treating residual drug as an intact pharmacy return.

choices.text: Record X as a partially administered patient dose to avoid entering any movement back to the pharmacy inventory.
choices.why: Incorrect. Fabricating an administration record would obscure an unused return and compromise controlled-substance inventory accountability.

items.citation: MA DPH General Accountability Guidelines for Controlled Substances in Hospitals and Clinics with Pharmacies, Nursing Units, Schedules II–V; 105 CMR 700.005
items.novelty_rationale: Discriminates custody transfer of an intact unused dose versus witnessed waste of partially used patient dose.

items.stem: A Massachusetts originating retail pharmacy and a properly licensed central-fill pharmacy operate a compliant shared-service arrangement. The central-fill pharmacy robot prepared several Schedule VI patient-specific packages, which have now arrived at the originating pharmacy for patient pickup. Before any patient handoff, the manufacturer announces a LOT-specific recall covering one package. The originating pharmacy wants to distribute that package and let the central-fill partner handle the recall later because the robot made it. What should the pharmacy do?

choices.text: Release the affected package because a central-fill robot, not the dispensing pharmacy, is responsible for product quality at preparation.
choices.why: Incorrect. Automation does not remove the originating or central-fill participants' joint shared-service responsibilities and patient safety duties.

choices.text: Hold the recalled lot and coordinate with central fill through the shared audit trail; release only an appropriate unaffected product.
choices.why: Correct. Under Board Policy 2021-02 each participant is jointly responsible for properly processed and filled orders, quality/safety, and traceable shared workflow; a known affected lot should not be released.

choices.text: Send the recalled package to the patient unopened with a note that the patient may request a replacement later.
choices.why: Incorrect. Knowingly distributing an affected recalled lot conflicts with product integrity, current recall duties and shared participant responsibility.

choices.text: Change the label's lot number to an unaffected one so the package can still be sold without altering the robot's completed record.
choices.why: Incorrect. Altering the package information does not change the physical drug lot or resolve the recall and compromises required audit records.

items.citation: MA Board Policy 2021-02 §§III(g)–(p), IV(a)–(b) (revised Feb. 6, 2025); 247 CMR 9.19(12) recall/quality duties
items.novelty_rationale: Central-fill physical production + robot + origin final release under a specific confirmed recall, not a generic remote-processing item.

items.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy will keep the SAME owner, manager of record, and staff but move its licensed dispensing operations to a NEW STREET ADDRESS. Management wants to treat the move as an ordinary online license renewal. The planned opening is 45 days away, and the Board has not granted an alternative application timetable or approved the new site. What is required before the pharmacy may operate at the new address?

choices.text: The pharmacy may move immediately, provided the current license is posted at the new premises and the Board receives notice within 14 days.
choices.why: Incorrect. 247 CMR 6.16 requires advance Board approval before relocating; moving is not merely a posting or after-the-fact notification task.

choices.text: The pharmacy may transfer the existing address registration without prior approval because the legal owner and manager have not changed.
choices.why: Incorrect. Same ownership and MOR do not eliminate the separate licensed-premises relocation application/approval requirement.

choices.text: Apply for Board relocation approval at least 90 days beforehand unless waived, and obtain approval before using the new address.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 6.16 explicitly requires a relocation application and payment, pharmacy layout drawings, and prior Board approval; the 90-day normal lead time may be varied by Board approval.

choices.text: Obtain DEA approval only; the Massachusetts Board has no separate role in approving a pharmacy's move to a new address.
choices.why: Incorrect. Controlled registration may be relevant but does not displace the Massachusetts relocation license rule.

items.citation: 247 CMR 6.16 (relocation application, 90-day normal lead time and prior approval); 247 CMR 6.15 (distinct remodel)
items.novelty_rationale: Premises relocation despite unchanged ownership and MOR, distinct from earlier closure/ownership/renovation cases.

author_note: All slots mapped to reserved IDs/competencies. Official source is an author citation pending item-specific adjudication; not an independent legal signoff.
